https://www.thetimes.com/article/shell-s.title: Shell sues Greenpeace for $2.1 million over North Sea oil protest
https://www.thetimes.com/article/shell-s.text:
Shell is suing Greenpeace for $2.1 million after activists from the environmental group occupied one of its vessels to protest against its North Sea oil drilling plans.
The oil major claimed that it had incurred significant costs after six Greenpeace activists boarded a ship carrying a floating production, storage and offloading vessel in January as it was en route to a shipyard in Norway. The activists occupied the vessel, which is ultimately intended for use at the Penguins field in the UK North Sea, for 13 days.
Shell said the protest had been extremely dangerous. It offered to drop the court action if Greenpeace paid it $1.4 million and agreed never to attempt to board or obstruct any Shell equipment at sea or in port ever again, according to email correspondence.
Greenpeace rejected this offer unless Shell agreed to cut its emissions in line with a court ruling in the Netherlands, against which Shell is appealing. It said negotiations had ended and it was now seeking emergency donations from supporters to help it to fight the case, which it described as “one of the biggest legal threats against the Greenpeace network’s ability to campaign in its more than 50-year history”.
It said it had been warned that the total claim against it could increase to $8.6 million if Fluor, the company that made the vessel, also decided to sue.
A spokesman for Shell said: “The right to protest is fundamental and we respect it absolutely but it must be done safely and lawfully. Boarding a 72,000 metric tonne moving vessel at sea was unlawful and extremely dangerous. A judge said Greenpeace protesters were ‘putting their lives and, indirectly, the lives of the crew at risk’.”
Shell is Europe’s biggest oil and gas group and made record profits of $40 billion last year. It procured the floating production, storage and offloading facility for use redeveloping the Penguins oil field in the northern UK North Sea. The field is expected to pump 45,000 barrels per day at peak.
The production vessel was loaded on board another vessel, the White Marlin, and was being transported from China to Norway by contractors for Shell when four Greenpeace activists boarded it near the Canary Islands on January 31. Two further activists boarded it while in the English Channel in early February.
One activist fell into the water while attempting to board the White Marlin and Shell argues that they could easily have been dragged under and seriously injured or killed had the vessel been turning in a different direction at the time.
Greenpeace disputes this, arguing that the activists were “wearing both commercial-grade immersion suits and life jackets which would have kept them buoyant at all times, preventing them from being dragged under”. A spokeswoman said it had rescue boats in the water and had “a very long track record of carrying out action at sea safely”.
Greenpeace disputes this version of events arguing that the activists were “wearing both commercial-grade immersion suits and life jackets which would have kept them buoyant at all times, preventing them from being dragged under”. A spokeswoman said it had rescue boats in the water and had “a very long track record of carrying out action at sea safely”.
A Shell spokesman said it had incurred “significant” legal costs securing two court injunctions to prevent further activists boarding the vessel, and significant costs also arose for “the companies who had to deal with the action at sea, for example by mobilising an extra safety vessel and increasing security at the port”.
“The safety of the protesters, as well as the crew, was paramount,” he said. “Rightly, we did not hesitate to put in place measures to protect all people involved. Shell and its contractors are entitled to recover the significant costs of responding to Greenpeace’s dangerous actions.”
Greenpeace said: “Aggressive legal tactics are a bid to silence growing dissent over chief executive Wael Sawan’s moves to double down on fossil fuel investment and abandon any pretence of transition to renewables.”
Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said that Sawan was “trying to crush Greenpeace’s ability to campaign, and in doing so, seeking to silence legitimate demands for climate justice and payment for loss and damage”.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/australas.title: Blinking heck: the cute koala is weaponised in Australian rightwingers’ anti-green fight
https://www.thetimes.com/world/australas.subtitle: 60,000 died in bushfires and Australia’s eco policies threaten many more
https://www.thetimes.com/world/australas.text:
Blinky the burning koala was unleashed in the aftermath of the Black Summer bushfires.
Hardline protesters from Extinction Rebellion staged a mock funeral in Melbourne in 2021 for their terrifying creation: a howling, smoking animatronic puppet, blackened fur stripped back to expose its skeleton.
More than 60,000 koalas died in the worst fires in years, among more than three billion animals killed or displaced.
The tree-dwelling marsupials were declared endangered last year, due to a combination of drought, disease and destruction of their habitat by developers and fire. Now many more of the creatures are at risk in the name of tackling climate change as thousands of acres of prime habitat are cleared to make way for vast wind and solar farms.
Koalas, visually appealing and uniquely Australian, have long been a staple of photo opportunities for ministers: the Australian equivalent of kissing a baby.
But it is the mounting sense of jeopardy about their future that has turned them into the ultimate Australian political animal, weaponised to highlight the perceived environmental shortcomings of the government of the day.
Koalas live in forests in much of Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and small parts of South Australia. They eat leaves from eucalyptus trees, which they shimmy up and down using their strong limbs, opposable thumbs and sharp claws. Their hard bottoms enable them to sit in forks of trees for long periods.
They also tend to live in some of the country’s more densely populated regions, where their habitat has been destroyed because trees have been cut down to make way for expanding town and city suburbs, or for farming and mining.
Their favourite haunts are often ideal sites for wind farms, which cannot be constructed too far from urban centres and are built in windier locations on hills or near the coast.
Today renewable energy projects are being fast-tracked by Labor state and federal governments to hit hugely ambitious net-zero carbon emissions targets. This includes a national target to obtain 82 per cent of the country’s energy from renewable sources by the end of the decade, before hitting net zero by 2050.
While public demand for more action to tackle climate change helped sweep Anthony Albanese’s Labor government to power 18 months ago, the rapid introduction of renewable energy hubs is facing a growing conservative backlash in regional Australia from farmers and those forced to live alongside them.
Rallies have sprung up at renewable energy building sites, some of them whipped up by the centre-right National Party, the junior member of the Liberal National coalition voted out of office in May last year.
The coalition has jumped at the chance to use the suffering of koalas to press its case. Opponents of the government have pounced on details contained in the “biodiversity management plan” for the Clarke Creek wind farm being constructed in central Queensland, backed by the iron-ore billionaire Andrew “Twiggy” Forrest.
The 125-page document stipulates that up to 3,738 acres of “core koala habitat” will have to be cleared, alongside a smaller area of forest inhabited by another endangered marsupial, the greater glider.
Gravely injured animals, it explained, may have to be euthanised with a “hard, sharp blow to the base of the back of the skull with a blunt metal or heavy wooden bar”. A Facebook post from the National’s coalition partners, the Liberal Party, featuring a picture of the energy minister Chris Bowen, reads: “Wind farms killing koalas, euthanasia will be conducted using blunt force trauma.”
Michelle Landry, a National MP who has led protests against the Clarke Creek wind farm in her Capricornia electorate, said the damage inflicted by huge solar and wind farms on rural communities, the landscape and native wildlife had been largely overlooked by the green movement.
“Our environment is being destroyed in the name of renewable energy,” she said. “People in the cities who think they are doing the right thing by supporting renewable just don’t realise what’s going on.”
Successive Australian prime ministers, including Albanese’s right-wing predecessor Scott Morrison, have committed millions of dollars to fund koala conservation projects while allowing large swathes of forest to be destroyed for mines, roads, railways and housing.
The Labor government has promised to overhaul the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, which has long been criticised for failing to protect wildlife. Under this legislation developers have routinely won approval to destroy habitats by using offsets, which typically involve cutting down trees and planting new ones elsewhere.
Australia still derives about two thirds of its electricity from coal and gas and is one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel exporters.
Bowen has said the 2030 target would require the installation of 40 giant wind turbines every month, 500 solar panels every day, and more than 6,000 miles of transmission lines to connect them to the grid.
Keith Pitt, another National MP and a former government resources minister, said the reluctance of many activists, Labor and Green party politicians to acknowledge the impact this would have on the landscape and native wildlife smacks of “hypocrisy”.
He said: “These protesters chain themselves to a coalmine to try to prevent coal being exported to the poorest people in India. But where are they on this?”
Squadron Energy, the developers of the Clarke Creek wind farm, said it had a “zero harm policy for native animals” and said no koalas had been injured or killed. It has also been pointed out that the Clarke Creek plans were approved long before Labor came power, having been signed off by Queensland’s Labor state government and the coalition government in 2018.
Despite being strident supporters of renewable energy, some conservation groups are warning that projects are too often being built on land teeming with wildlife, while developers are ignoring concerns from locals.
Queensland Conservation Council has calculated that the wind farms in the state awaiting federal government approval will require the destruction of more than 27,000 acres of koala habitat, and more than 13,500 acres of habitat of the endangered northern and greater glider. This includes the 94-turbine Chalumbin wind farm that would border a World Heritage-listed rainforest west of Cairns in the north of the state.

image.caption: A plan to clear koala habitat for turbines sets out how to kill any injured animalsGETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: The 28 cars that changed Jeremy Clarkson’s life
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
I have always loved cars. I could say “Maserati” before I could say “Mummy”. I would go to bed every night and peer for hours at the drawings in my Ladybird Book of Motor Cars, and when my dad, a travelling salesman, came home after a week or two on the road, he’d always bring me the latest model from Corgi or Dinky.
I was especially fond of the Citroën Le Dandy Coupé (1), which sits even now on a shelf in my new house. And the Buick Riviera (2), with jewelled headlights that flashed when you put your finger over the rear window. And the king of them all, the bright orangeAlfa Romeo OSI Scarabeo (3).
The highlight of my year was our annual pilgrimage to the Cathedral of Turtle Wax, otherwise known as the Earls Court Motor Show. My dad and I would stay at a small hotel in nearby Barkston Gardens and have some impossibly exotic spaghetti at the Palio restaurant on the Earls Court Road. And then the next morning, after a night bathed in breathless anticipation, I’d be there bright and early to collect as many brochures as possible. Which I’d then cut up to make a collage on my bedroom wall.
My first actual car was a ten-year-old Ford Cortina 1600E (4) and when I wasn’t driving it I could be found washing it and making fur door linings and removing the black paint from the Rostyle wheels and adding more lights and a graphic equaliser. And eventually a set of Wolfrace seats.
One day I fitted the engine with a chromed sports air filter and convinced my friends that it added another 100 horsepower. They would talk about their cars and then the sun would come up and we’d all drive home because none of us drank back then. Going to the pub wasn’t about the pub. It was about the drive there and back.
Naturally I wanted to work with cars, but this was likely to be a problem because I’m mathematically backward and less practically minded than a Californian fentanyl enthusiast, so engineering was out of the question. I also had another problem. Everything I ever draw looks like a dog, so I knew I’d never be a stylist, and I was too much of a sporting spanner to be much cop as a racing driver. However, I could write.
By which I mean I could spell. I had also won a poetry prize at school, and after three years on the Rotherham Advertiser and two block release courses in Sheffield, I had a piece of paper from the National Council for the Training of Journalists that said I’d passed the relevant exams and was therefore a qualified hack. Which, in my mind, made me Bob Woodward.
I therefore wrote to a chap called Steve Cropley, who was editing Car magazine at the time, letting him know that I was available. And he kindly wrote back thanking me for keeping him in the loop, but inviting me to go away.
I then applied for jobs with every other car magazine and when that didn’t work either I wrote to all of the advertising agencies that had a car account, asking for a job in their copywriting department. This appealed to my fundamental laziness because when you review a car for a magazine you have to write thousands of words, whereas in an advert you just have to come up with “Coke is it” and then go for lunch. I mean “Vorsprung durch Technik”. Those creative boys didn’t even bother translating that into English.
All the agencies had me in for an interview and afterwards all of them invited me to go away as well. So I ended up getting a job as a travelling salesman for my mum and dad’s toy company.
It wasn’t exactly what I’d had in mind, but my company car was a Volkswagen Scirocco GLi (5) — 1,588cc, Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection — which I’d ruined by fitting tyres that were so wide the steering wheel felt as though it was set in cement.
I loved that car like I loved my ability to move about and see things. And what I loved most is that Car magazine said it did 0 to 60 in 8.1 seconds, which made me more of a man than Andy Scott, whose Vauxhall Chevette HS 2.3 (6) took 8.3 seconds. Weirdly, girls used to find our discussions about this quite uninteresting.
It turned out that I was a terrible salesman. I’d walk into a toyshop and ask the owner if he’d like to buy a stuffed dog or maybe a preposterous 3ft-tall felt Captain Beaky. He’d say “No” and I’d say “OK” and that would be that.
But the job did at least mean I could do a huge amount of driving. I’d get up. Drive to Swansea. Discover that no one wanted a stuffed dog or a 3ft-tall felt bird. And then I’d drive home again. And the next day I’d go to Dorchester and repeat the process, before heading off the following day to King’s Lynn to learn that no one there wanted my wares either. In my first year on the job I sold absolutely nothing at all, but I covered 54,000 wonderful, exciting and liberating miles in my beloved Scirocco.
When I got back to London I’d drive it some more. Before the killjoy-in-chief installed traffic lights at Hyde Park Corner, I’d meet up with my like-minded mates and we’d take it in turns to see how many people we could get to blow their horns at us in a single lap of the traffic island. Geoff always won, once with a blistering sideways lap in his blue metalflake Alfa Romeo GTA (7), where he scored a massive 14 honks.
And then, the next morning, I was back in the car and off for another pointless foray into the dying world of stuffed toy retail.
Then, one day, while sitting at the lights in an Oxfordshire town called Wallingford, I noticed the local newspaper offices and wondered if they had a motoring column. It seemed unlikely. So then I began to wonder if maybe any local paper had one. And later, as a man in the local toyshop told me he wasn’t interested in my stuffed dog or the felt bird, a thought struck me.
If I reviewed a car, I could send the same review to a hundred papers all round the country. They’d get a well-written (well, well-spelt) review for maybe £20, which made it good value for them. And I’d get £2,000 a week for doing something I wanted to do anyway. In the pub I told my friend Jonathan Gill about this wheeze and the next morning, instead of driving to Wednesbury, I resigned from the toy industry, went to Prontaprint, bought some headed paper and in the front room of Jonathan’s house the Motoring Press Agency was born.
It was a disaster. It turned out that a great many local newspapers did in fact have a motoring correspondent and that he took umbrage at any attempt to dislodge him from what he saw as a cushy number. Also, we quickly discovered that most local newspapers were part of large groups that had access to centralised features on travel, home improvement, fashion and cars.
To make matters worse, it turned out my poor selling technique wasn’t limited to soft toys. I’d ring the editor of the Black Country Bugle, ask him if he’d like a car review every week for £20, he’d say “No” and I’d say “OK” and that would be that. Again.
To make it even worse, I was experiencing the misery and humiliation of not being any good as a salesman and not even having a long drive to look forward to afterwards. There was nothing for it. Jonathan and I repaired to the White Horse in Fulham and pretty much lived there for a year.
We’d occasionally pop back to his house to watch Danger Mouse, and in the evening we’d go to the Shahin on the Fulham Road for a chicken madras. Then I’d trudge back to the Vomitorium, the house I was renting with three mates. Actually, two mates and a man who got up very early every morning and sat in the bath listening to Radio 4. Which is not what you need when you’ve been at the pub all day and have a headache.
It was called the Vomitorium because that’s mostly what we did in it. After a couple of months things were so bad that you could never stand still for very long or you’d stick to the carpet.
Incredibly, though, after just two years the Motoring Press Agency was flying. Mainly thanks to Jonathan, we’d secured a number of accounts, including the Shropshire Star, a newspaper on Humberside and Lincolnshire Life, which once changed “Aston Martin” throughout a review I’d written to “Austin Martin”.
The cash was dizzying. In year three, once we’d split the income evenly and deducted the cost of our photography, we each took home £1,600. Which today would be £6,400. And that is what Sir Starmer would call “well below the poverty line for hard-working people in the community”.
You wouldn’t have guessed it, though, if you’d seen how we were living. Because we had a few outlets for our reviews we could borrow cars from the manufacturers, which would be delivered every week full of fuel and fully insured. So I was going to work in a Renault Fuego Turbo (8) or an Alfa GTV6 (9) or a Toyota Supra (10) and it was costing me nothing.
And that was just the start of it. Twice a week we’d be invited to a “press launch”, which meant flying to Cannes or Madrid or Rome, staying at the best hotel, eating the finest and completely free food and, the next day, driving whatever car was being launched on the best roads the company’s PR team had been able to find. I got to know La Réserve in Beaulieu so well the doorman recognised me. Not in my wildest dreams had I ever thought such a job even existed.
Daihatsu once invited me to go to Japan and try out a new little buzz bomb called the Charade GTti (11). This meant flying first class on Cathay Pacific to Hong Kong, spending a couple of all-expenses-paid days at the five-star Regent hotel before heading northeast in great luxury to Kyoto. Here, I climbed into the car and immediately crashed it. And having been told not to worry because “we make one every 23 seconds” I flew first class again, to Hawaii, where our little group spent a couple of days jet-skiing around Maui before heading off, at the front of yet another 747 obviously, to San Francisco for a long weekend at the Fairmont on Nob Hill.
Then I came home to find I couldn’t afford to pay the bill for the long-term parking at Heathrow. I was living a life Elton John could only dream about while earning even less than Sir Keir Starmer’s dad, who — in case you’ve been on Jupiter for the past five years — was a toolmaker.
And then it all came crashing down. I was at the launch of the Citroën AX (12) at a fancy spa hotel full of wet idiots in sliders and, over lunch, found myself sitting next to a man who had Jay Leno’s chin and Brian Sewell’s accent. It turned out he was called Jon Bentley and he was a producer on the BBC show Top Gear.
A month later he called and asked me to do a screen test, so I prepared something about a Range Rover (13). But Jon produced a Citroën 2CV (14) and with no warning asked me to do something on that as well. It’s strange when you first talk on television, because when the director said “Action”, I suddenly became aware, for the first time in my life, of my hands — and they were enormous. It was as if I had two marrows on the ends of my arms and, to make everything worse, each of the 40 muscles in my throat had started to spasm, causing me to swallow constantly. Still, I spoke for two minutes about ladies with sturdy shoes, whales and Monsignor Bruce Kent, and despite being Edward Marrowhands I got the gig.
This meant I had to be available at short notice for filming duties, which meant I could no longer realistically spend quite so many balmy evenings on the terrace in St Tropez drinking Château Pétrus. But at least the pay was awful. I was offered £180 a day and in the first year earned £360.
But, and this is the kicker, what the Top Gear job meant was: I was now first in line to try all the hot cars and the speed machines. I was the kid who’d gone to sleep after playing with his Alfa Scarabeo and reading his Ladybird Book of Motor Cars, in a bedroom festooned with glossy car pictures, and now I was going to be driving this sort of stuff on TV.
It took a while. Some of the old guard at Pebble Mill saw no reason to review cars that “people can’t afford”, but I pointed out that most people couldn’t afford an Austin Metro either. “So if you are going to review cars that are out of most people’s price range, they might as well be very out of their price range because at least that way they’d be exciting to look at.”
And so it was, without actually getting permission as such, that I spent a breathless couple of days with a director called Dennis Jarvis filming every single Lamborghini we could lay our hands on. We had a Miura (15) and an LM002 (16), and we raced a Diablo (17) against a Golf GTi (18) to demonstrate the difference between a fast car and a Lambo, and we used Pulnix minicams on the end of the sound man’s mike pole and a Bad Company soundtrack, and the bosses were appalled. But we’d spent so much money making the film, they sort of had to show it.
And it worked. It turned out the country was rammed with people like me who liked fast cars, so Top Gear did an immediate handbrake turn. And instead of William Woollard signing off at the end of the programme saying, “Well, that’s another show done, as it were. Next week we’re heavily into second-hand cars, basically in Nottingham. Lots and lots of good advice to pick up if you want to. Until then. See you then. Drive safely. Goodnight,” we had me driving round a corner too quickly on full opposite lock asking viewers to drive fast.
I was captain of the toybox and I ended up going round the world, making shows about motoring culture and jets and speedboats and this all culminated, in 2002, with the birth of new Top Gear, with the Stig, Richard Hammond and, eventually, James May. Which, after Top Gear became the most-watched TV show in the world, gave rise to that monstrous opening for The Grand Tour in the California desert.
And then …
Even until quite recently you only had to show me a small part of a car, an indicator lens or a door handle and usually I’d be able to tell you immediately not just which sort of car it was and which model, but quite often which model derivative. An L, a GL or a GT.
I used to entertain myself on the motorway at night by looking at a car’s tail lights from half a mile away and seeing if I could work out what it was before I caught it up. And I could. Never wrong.
Now, though, you could stand me in a car park in broad daylight and point at a modern-day SUV thing that is 10ft away and I wouldn’t have a clue. I went to Silverstone this year for the grand prix and was ferried across the circuit in a car that was blue. That’s all I can tell you.
And there’s more. When I was 18 I literally could not drive past a stubble field without being overcome with a wave of uncontrollable desire to go into it and spend a few minutes doing skids. Now? I have stubble fields of my own and the impetus has gone. Drive round in them for fun? I’d rather roll around in them naked.
It’s the same story on the road. I used to blast past everyone all the time. But now I drive at whatever speed the vehicle in front is doing, and that’s fine by me. I was even overtaken recently, which I’m fairly sure has never happened before, and I didn’t mind. It didn’t dent my ego. I may even have muttered “maniac” as the hearse went past.
Age is partly responsible for a lot of this and there’s no question I’ve spent a very long time in the chocolate factory. When you can drive pretty much anything that takes your fancy, it does eventually become dull. That’s why Warren Beatty became gay. Actually, I’m not sure he did become gay, but I bet he did reach a point where he said, “No, Carly, you cannot bring Raquel over tonight. I want to press flowers instead.”
And when it comes to losing interest in cars, I’m not alone. Young people, and especially young men, have always loved cars. But today that love seems to be on the wane. Many don’t even bother to get a licence, saying they’d rather use Uber and that coaches have free wi-fi. Some of this, I’m sure, is down to Gen Z’s obsession with net zero Just Stop Oil ecoism, but there must be more to it than that. It takes more than one snot-nosed Swedish kid to end our century-old love affair with the car.
Unless she’s being actively aided and abetted by the car industry itself. And she is.
Carmakers have always been forced to make small, economical cars for people who didn’t have much spare cash at the end of the month. But they did their best to make those small cars interesting. Which is why we got the original Mini (19) and the Citroën 2CV and the Fiat 500 (20), and even as recently as the Nineties the Daihatsu Charade GTti. I didn’t drive it for very long in Japan before I crashed it, but I do remember being amazed that something with a one-litre engine could produce more than a hundred horsepower. That really was people power.
But now look at what they’re giving us. Look at that ridiculous electric Citroën AMI (21). I’m not sure that even qualifies as a car. And then examine the bestselling cars in the UK so far this year: the Ford Puma (22), the Nissan Kumquat (23) and the Vauxhall Corsa (24). There’s nothing there to titillate a small boy’s underpant zone. There isn’t even a fast version of any of them. And the fourth bestseller is a bloody Tesla Model Y (25). Which is basically a kettle.
Couple this to the fact that if the car were invented today, no government in the world would allow normal people to drive it. They’d say it was too dangerous for ordinary mortals. Which is why they’re all so hell bent on Ulez and net zero and making sure that the small number of teenagers who want to take a driving test can’t.
I don’t mind, though, because my God I lucked out on the timing. I was there in 1971 when music reached its zenith and Hunky Dory, Who’s Next and Led Zeppelin IV were all released within months of one another. I was there when comedians were allowed to be funny and television was a smorgasbord of gems such as Blackadder and Fawlty Towers. And my time as a petrolhead sits neatly between the bookends of the first Ford Mustang (26) and the last Nissan GT-R (27).
Plus, by the time they get round to making driving so difficult it will no longer be worth anyone’s while, I’ll be landfill. Just remember to put a picture of that Alfa Scarabeo in my coffin. And at the funeral play a soundtrack of the Lexus LFA (28) at full chat.
Calling all car sleuths. Clarkson’s first car was a 1969 Ford Cortina MkII 1600E, registration number AWT 610G, with fur-lined doors and racing seats. His dad also had a MkII Cortina. “I didn’t know there were other cars,” Clarkson says. “I was raised in a Ford Cortina.” But where is Jeremy’s first car? A number plate check suggests it’s still in existence. It hasn’t been scrapped or exported, nor has it been declared an insurance write-off. It’s listed as originally gold in colour — although it could since have been resprayed. If it’s out there, we want to find it and we need your help. Write to magazine@sunday-times.co.uk, preferably with a photo of the car, or post in the online comments.

image.caption: Clarkson at Diddly Squat Farm comparing a real limited edition Ford GT with a model Ford GT40 from his childhoodTOM BARNES FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES MAGAZINE

https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.title: Climate activists glue 50 Barclays branches shut
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.subtitle: Money Rebellion wants customers to boycott the bank because it invests in fossil fuel projects
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.text:
A group linked to Extinction Rebellion has forced the closure of 50 branches of Barclays Bank after activists superglued their doors shut.
Supporters of Money Rebellion, a “sister organisation” of XR, disabled the entrances of branches in Tottenham Court Road in London, Kilmarnock Road in Glasgow and Albion Street in Leeds.
Activists urged customers to boycott the company to exert pressure on Barclays to stop funding fossil fuel projects.
The bank has previously been targeted by Greenpeace, which claims it is the largest funder of fossil fuels in Europe. It has demanded the bank switch to supporting renewable energy projects.
A spokesman for Money Rebellion said the disruption was “part of a significant new wave of property-focused climate action. Climate change is real and happening now. We urge Barclays customers to use their power by moving their account to a bank more aligned with a liveable future for the planet.”
According to Bank.Green, which campaigns for banks to fund green projects, Barclays has invested $190.6 billion in fossil fuels in the seven years since the Paris agreement on climate change.
Barclays has previously said it will stop financing all oil sands and tar sands companies as well as new oil sands pipelines.
A Money Rebellion activist who took part in the action said: “Barclays are pumping billions into the fossil fuel industry, completely at odds with advice from the International Energy Agency, United Nations and Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Barclays are choosing short-term profits over a liveable future and a lot of us are sick of the measly progress they’re making, as they hide behind their lies and greenwash.”
An XR activist added: “We’re responding to public attitudes and targeting the perpetrators of climate breakdown, not ordinary people and we apologise for any inconvenience caused to staff and customers. The inconvenience we’ve caused this morning is small in comparison to the catastrophic events already happening due to Barclays’ financing of fossil fuels.”
A Barclays spokesperson said: “Aligned to our ambition to be a net zero bank by 2050, we believe we can make the greatest difference by working with our clients as they transition to a low-carbon business model, reducing their carbon-intensive activity whilst scaling low-carbon technologies, infrastructure and capacity.
“We have set 2030 targets to reduce the emissions we finance in five high-emitting sectors, including the energy sector, where we have achieved a 32 per cent reduction since 2020. In addition, to scale the needed technologies and infrastructure, we have provided £99 billion of green finance since 2018, and have a target to facilitate $1 trillion in sustainable and transition financing between 2023 and 2030.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/the-.title: The Times view on Armistice Day march: Respecting Protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/the-.text:
Probably scores, and maybe hundreds, of thousands of demonstrators will converge on London today to protest against Israel’s military action in Gaza. They have the right in a free society to do so, and the Metropolitan Police have the corresponding responsibility of ensuring the demonstration proceeds in an orderly and peaceful way. And, contrary to a spirited intervention by Suella Braverman, the home secretary, in our pages this week, it is crucial that the Met and its commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, be trusted to judge how best to do this without any political interference.
Yet the vital principle of operational independence of policing is not the end of the matter. If the Met is to retain civic legitimacy, it must be seen to be politically impartial. Ms Braverman’s intervention may have been clumsy but it was not baseless. The Met’s policing of protests in recent times has veered between harshness against unthreatening assembly and perplexing indulgence of demonstrable lawlessness. It needs to strike a more thoughtful balance today, in which the optimal mix is a light touch towards legitimate protest while firmly preventing access to such symbolically important sites as the Cenotaph.
The protesters’ message is intrinsically misguided. Humanitarian concern for the citizens of Gaza and support for a Palestinian state alongside Israel are just causes but these protests acknowledge neither the barbarism of Hamas’s assault on civilians on October 7 nor Israel’s right of self-defence. When British Jews, especially those of university age, feel threatened by the recrudescence of antisemitism, decent people must stand with them.
The Met must police, rather than suppress, today’s protest. And while Ms Braverman has earned criticism for pre-emptively referring to the demonstrators collectively as “mobs”, protecting the public will require coercion as well as consent. Every demonstration attracts extremists, and the pro-Palestine protests of the past month have been visibly suffused with placards from the Socialist Workers’ Party, a virulently antisemitic far-left organisation that urges the state of Israel be “smashed”. The protest organisers may give assurances the procession will avoid the Cenotaph but they lack influence over this fringe.
Indeed, the very act of protest on the weekend of Remembrance Sunday may be lawful under the Human Rights Act and Public Order Act, but is still lamentable. Jeremy Corbyn, the former Labour leader, crassly said this week the demonstrations would be “part and parcel” of the occasion, as if the act of remembrance were a pacifist rally rather than an expression of gratitude for those who took up arms in just war against tyranny.
The risk for the Met under these circumstances is that it will appear not so much partial as weak and vacillating. This inconsistency is bound to drain public confidence. Memories are vivid of the police’s insensitive handling of an unofficial vigil in south London in 2021 for Sarah Everard, for whose abduction and murder Wayne Couzens, a Met officer, was later jailed with a full-life tariff. Protests against lockdowns and under the banner of “Black Lives Matter” took place roughly simultaneously, and in apparent defiance of pandemic restrictions, with no such hindrance. Vandalism in museums by Just Stop Oil protesters is frequent.
The rule of law is fundamental to a free society, and so is the right of free assembly. Maintaining the proper balance between them is the preserve not of the home secretary but of the police. If such judgments were left to politicians, there would be no inherent limit on their ability to hamstring and even persecute opposition parties. But the police need to provide reassurance to the wider community of their safety as well as ensure that protests are protected. Sir Mark and the Met have not yet won that consent. This weekend’s events will be a test of how far they have managed to do so.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.title: Greta Thunberg appears in court over London protest
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.subtitle: Climate activist pleads not guilty to public order offence
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.text:
Greta Thunberg has pleaded not guilty to committing a public order offence at a protest outside a hotel in central London that was hosting heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies.
The Swedish environmental activist is one of 26 people who were charged after a demonstration last month outside the InterContinental London hotel on Park Lane, which was hosting the annual Energy Intelligence Forum, an oil industry conference.
Activists at the demonstration, which was organised by Fossil Free London, blocked access to the hotel, while others lit flares. Protesters from Greenpeace abseiled down from the roof to unfurl a banner reading: “Make big oil pay.”
Thunberg, 20, was led away from the hotel by Metropolitan Police officers, who arrested 29 people in total. Supporters shouted “thank you, Greta” as she was being searched.
The environmental activist appeared in court accused of breaching Section 14 of the Public Order Act by failing to leave the highway and continuing her protest on the street.
During the 20-minute hearing the activist appeared alongside four other environmental campaigners, all of whom pleaded not guilty to failing to comply with a condition imposed under Section 14.
Thunberg was given unconditional bail ahead of a three-day trial at City of London magistrates’ court on February 1 next year.
Thunberg, who appeared in court wearing a grey top, jeans and white boots, laughed several times with other activists while waiting for the judge to arrive.
She was mobbed by photographers as she entered the court, spent 20 minutes getting through security and sat on the floor outside the court with her supporters before the hearing.
The court heard that the activists were arrested after a senior police officer imposed restrictions on the protest, requiring it to be moved to the pavement.
The maximum sentence for failing to comply with Section 14 of the Public Order Act is six months’ imprisonment and a £2,500 fine.
Thunberg was surrounded by a large crowd of photographers and video journalists as she left Westminster magistrates’ court. She walked along the pavement but after failing to break free from the cluster she sharply changed direction and sprinted away down Marylebone Road.
The day after she was charged with the public order offence, Thunberg joined fellow activists outside the Canary Wharf offices of JP Morgan and Barclays. The demonstration, which was also organised by Fossil Free London, claimed that fossil fuel companies were deliberately slowing the global transition to renewable energy to make more profit.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Ambulance held up in Just Stop Oil Waterloo Bridge protest
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Police arrest dozens of climate activists staging a slow march
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
A London paramedic on a “life and death” emergency call begged police to make way for an ambulance as Just Stop Oil blocked Waterloo Bridge.
Activists for the environmental group performed a slow march on the thoroughfare, causing police to close it in both directions on Wednesday morning.
An ambulance arrived with blue lights and sirens but was held up in traffic for ten minutes.
The driver of the ambulance told The Telegraph: “I am responding to a life-and-death emergency — I am going to pick up a team from Guy’s hospital to save someone’s life at another hospital but can’t get through.”
The newspaper reported that the paramedic, part of Guy’s and St Thomas’ ECMO Retrieval Team which helps people whose lungs have stopped working and need urgent care, pleaded with officers to allow him to pass as he became visibly angry. Police said they were working to let him through as protesters lay on the road.
The group said it expected most of the 55 activists taking part in the march to be arrested under the Public Order Act 2023.
A spokesman for Just Stop Oil said: “Earlier today, the Metropolitan Police shared a tweet suggesting that Just Stop Oil supporters were blocking an ambulance vehicle. We have deep sympathy for anyone suffering a medical emergency at any time. Nobody’s life or health is more valuable than others.
“Just Stop Oil’s ‘Blue Lights’ policy has always been that we immediately move out of the way for emergency vehicles with blue lights on. The London Ambulance Service has previously confirmed via Freedom of Information requests that there has been no significant disruption to ambulances as a result of Just Stop Oil actions.
“In this case, Just Stop Oil supporters were on the other side of the road, and had never blocked the side of the road the ambulance was on. The picture shared by the Metropolitan Police indicates that it’s only their officers who are blocking the road with the ambulance. Our own pictures confirm this.
“Nevertheless, we accept that our actions do cause disruption. There are a limited range of options available to normal people to resist government criminality. We will not stand by and watch while our government continues to license new oil and gas, which in itself is an act of violence.”
One of those on the road this morning, Geraldine Swift, 57, an NHS consultant psychiatrist, said: “I am a passionate and persistent moderate who believes in the rule of law, but this cannot be an absolute – we can all think of bad laws in the past, and bad decisions made by governments.
“We are in a climate and health emergency now: this is what the science tells us, the United Nations and my college, the Royal College of Psychiatrists.”
The London Ambulance Service said: “An ambulance with a patient on board was delayed on Waterloo Bridge at 10.22am this morning. Fortunately, the ambulance crew was able to divert to a different hospital. However, delays can cost lives. We would ask any protesters to allow our crews to pass to ensure we are able to get timely treatment for our patients.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/pro-pal.title: Police slammed over pro-Palestine protest at Liverpool Street station
https://www.thetimes.com/article/pro-pal.subtitle: Jewish group and think tank said new law should have been used to break up sit-in
https://www.thetimes.com/article/pro-pal.text:
Police were criticised on Wednesday for failing to clamp down on pro-Palestinian activists who blockaded a train station as protests linked to the Middle Eastern conflict were held across the country.
While Scotland Yard released images of a dozen activists wanted for alleged criminality at rallies, British Transport Police (BTP) was accused of “complete acquiescence” over a sit-in at Liverpool Street.
About 500 activists blockaded the station during rush hour on Tuesday night chanting “ceasefire now”, while some shouted “from the river to the sea”. BTP were asked why they did not deploy protest legislation, created this year to prevent Just Stop Oil disrupting national infrastructure.
The Met issued a public appeal to identify 12 people suspected of offences at pro-Palestine protests in central London on October 14 and 28. Images were distributed on social media. The dozen are wanted for alleged offences of affray and racially aggravated alarm, harassment and distress.
West Midlands police have arrested a 32-year-old man and appealed for information on a second, called Billal Hussain, 30, after mice dyed in the colours of the Palestinian flag were released at McDonald’s restaurants in Birmingham on Monday and Tuesday.
The force said the incidents are being treated as public nuisances.
Another branch was hit by a third attack at 9pm yesterday when masked men entered a restaurant in Small Heath, chanted “Free Palestine” and waved the Palestinian flag and threw a box containing live mice towards staff. Police are investigating the third incident and are unclear if it is connected to the previous two incidents. McDonald’s, which was targeted after a branch in Israel offered discounts to soldiers, said it was dismayed by “disinformation and inaccurate reports regarding our position in response to the conflict in the Middle East”.
Video was shared online showing pro-Palestinian protesters outside a Marks & Spencer store in Glasgow, while more than 200 people staged another sit-in on the concourse at London Waterloo station on Saturday.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism questioned why police had not intervened at Liverpool Street under Section 7 of the Public Order Act 2023, which criminalises deliberate disruption to national infrastructure. It added: “We have heard from Jewish Londoners who arrived at the station and felt they had to turn back.”
The sit-in was organised by Sisters Uncut, a feminist group. It said it had chosen Liverpool Street station due to its connection to the City of London, “notorious for funnelling arms trade money through it”. The group cited banks it said invested in the arms trade with Israel, adding: “Crossrail is currently advising the Israeli government on building a national transit service.”
BTP said that services were not disrupted. However, David Spencer, head of crime and justice at the think tank Policy Exchange, said that the station protest was “clearly a breach” of new legislation designed to thwart environmental activities. He criticised the “complete acquiescence” of BTP, saying the Public Order Act 2023 prevents the disruption of rail infrastructure.
Spencer, a former police officer, told The Times: “BTP’s statement is at best an effort to pretend it wasn’t all that bad and at worst a message of total surrender to the rule of the mob over the rule of law.” BTP did not respond to questions about why it had not used public order legislation but said anyone wishing to make a report could text 61016 or call 0800 40 50 40.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/dutch-e.title: Does the Netherlands have a refugee problem? The key election issue
https://www.thetimes.com/article/dutch-e.text:
This article was originally published on November 5, before the 2023 Dutch elections.
For more than five decades the cruise liner Ocean Majesty sailed the world’s seas, most recently taking elderly German holidaymakers to the edge of the Arctic Circle. Since August, however, it has found a more humble berth: the docks in Velsen-Noord, a Dutch village about 30 kilometres northwest of Amsterdam. The ship has seen more glamorous days: the swimming pool has been drained and taped off, the duty-free shop filled with donated clothes and toys, and the Bellini Bar, where passengers used to drink cocktails and smoke cigars, is used for Dutch lessons.
The Greek-owned vessel, built in the mid-1960s, has been given a new life as part of attempts by the Dutch government to cope with the number of refugees pouring into what is already one of the most densely populated countries in the world. Up to 300 people now live on the ship: they are among some 6,000 housed on water across the Netherlands — on two repurposed Estonian ferries, the Silja Europa, which is docked in Rotterdam, and the Silja Galaxy, in Amsterdam, as well as almost two dozen smaller river cruise boats. Before the end of the year another 1,000 will be accommodated on two “floating motels”, the Bibby Progress and Bibby Renaissance — sister ships of Britain’s controversial Bibby Stockholm. The flotilla was hastily drafted into service just over a year ago after chronic overcrowding forced hundreds of asylum seekers at the main Dutch reception centre in Ter Apel, close to the German border, to sleep outside in appalling conditions.
Although it is going nowhere, the ship remains under the command of Ioannis Antoniou, its veteran captain and his crew of more than 70. Antoniou was surprised when he was informed about his new role and admits he would rather be at sea. “But I am a professional and I follow my company’s orders,” he says, resplendent in his neatly pressed white uniform. “It’s a challenge but I also feel good because I am helping these people who have come from some difficult places.”
There could be no more poignant symbol of the migration crisis faced by the Netherlands, which is at the sharp end of the crisis confronting Europe as whole. Last year a record 403,108 immigrants arrived — 150,580 more than in 2021, according to figures from Statistics Netherlands. This number — of which 257,522 were other Europeans, including 108,000 Ukrainians fleeing the war in their country — was twice as high as during the migrant crisis of 2015.
It was a row over immigration that caused the collapse of the Dutch government in July, prompting Mark Rutte, 56, prime minister since 2010, to announce his retirement from politics. The problem is likely to be a key issue in the general election on November 22 that will decide who will become the next prime minister.
The growing number of arrivals has provoked a broader debate about how many more people can be squeezed into the Netherlands — a debate that has, in turn, become entangled with the government’s faltering attempts to cut greenhouse gas emissions sufficiently to achieve net zero by 2050. Nor is it just about people: it overlaps with an equally incendiary row over how many cows and pigs can live on Dutch soil, how many houses, roads and factories can be built and how many flights can land at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport.
At its heart is a simple question — does the country have too many people? — that inspired the title of a six-part series screened this time last year on Dutch television, The Netherlands Is Full. The answer holds lessons not just for the Dutch but also for other developed countries including Britain.
My first stop in the Netherlands is the Hague, officially the country’s most densely populated city. There are plenty of high-rise buildings around the main station where my Eurostar train pulls in, most of them dating from the past few decades, but lots of fairly low-rise ones too. People are not as crammed in as they are in New York or Paris, let alone the city-state of Monaco, the world’s most densely populated country.
This, though, is the heart of the Randstad — literally City on the Edge — the name for the urban sprawl also including Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Utrecht that is home to almost half of the country’s 17.8 million or so residents. Rents have been surging here almost as fast as they have been in southeast England, fuelling popular discontent. The need to find somewhere to house the migrants is adding to the problem. Appropriately enough, it was in the parliament here in 1950 that Queen Juliana in her Troonrede (speech from the throne), written by the government of the day, sounded the alarm about overcrowding. “Strong population growth and the limited availability of land continue to require strong encouragement of emigration,” she declared. At the time the population had just reached ten million.
In the event, 620,000 people left during the 1950s for new lives in Australia, Canada, New Zealand and America — although they were largely offset by the arrival of 490,000 immigrants, many of them Dutch nationals who left the Dutch East Indies after the former colony Indonesia’s declaration of independence. In Juliana’s last such speech in 1979 — by which time the population had reached 14 million — she reiterated the sentiment, declaring: “Our country is full, partly overcrowded.”
During the postwar years population growth had been driven by the Netherlands’ high birth rate, which at its peak in the early 1960s reached three children per woman, far more than in neighbouring countries. The number has since fallen to the European average of 1.5 — way below the replacement rate — but the shortfall has been more than made up for by immigration. At first this was predominantly from southern Europe; more recently it has been Poles and others from eastern EU states, as well as those from the Middle East or Africa fleeing persecution or searching for a better life.
The cumulative effect has been dramatic: since 1950 the population has risen by 78 per cent, compared with 55 per cent in France and 35 per cent in Britain. The recent focus has inevitably been on the sharp jump in the number of asylum applications, which reached 35,535 last year — 44 per cent more than in 2021 and the highest number since 2015 — with 10,925 more family members joining the asylum seekers. It has been predicted that the combined number could hit 70,000 this year.
It was the government’s attempts to stem this flow that precipitated the downfall of Rutte, a former Unilever executive who had survived so many scandals during his long political career he was nicknamed “Teflon Mark”. The crisis a year earlier at Ter Apel had pushed the issue of migration to centre stage: after a three-month old baby died there (the cause of death was not known) Rutte admitted the situation was “shameful” and ordered a raft of measures to try to bring things under control. As part of a toughening of asylum policy, his centre-right People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) had wanted to cap the number of family reunifications. But two of the four parties in his coalition objected on humanitarian grounds and the government, Rutte’s fourth, collapsed.
In the past the Dutch have made space for rapidly growing numbers by reclaiming vast tracts of land from the sea. The most dramatic example of this is Flevoland, an area almost the size of Dorset or Derbyshire that until a few decades ago was about five metres under water. It has since been transformed into farming land and is now home to 444,700 people, of whom 222,800 live in Almere. Built on the clay and sand of what was once seabed, this is now the eighth largest city in the Netherlands — and the fastest growing. I took the 20-minute train from Amsterdam to take a look.
Paul Meekel, who works as a tour guide, showed me around Almere’s city centre, an extraordinary architectural showpiece designed by some of the biggest names from around the world, including Britain’s William Alsop, on the basis of a template by Rem Koolhaas. One of its inspirations was the garden city movement, pioneered by Ebenezer Howard, the late 19th-century British town planner. Think a more stylish version of Milton Keynes, with which Almere has been partnered — though with real rather than concrete cows.
As we walked, Meekel pointed out signs on the sides of buildings far above our heads marking what used to be sea level. “It began with 20 families living down near the harbour in the early 1970s,” he says. “The Dutch government has now commissioned us to grow further until we have something like 350,000 inhabitants.” The next stage in Almere’s extraordinary expansion includes an ambitious plan for 500 floating houses in Pampus Harbour, just off Flevoland’s west coast, facing Amsterdam.
Although Flevoland is impressive, it is not a shortage of land that prevents the Netherlands from accommodating all the newcomers. The country is certainly densely populated, with 522 people per square kilometre, compared with 434 for England, or just 279 if you add Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. As in the UK, however, the population is unevenly spread: the province of South Holland, in which the most densely populated part of the Randstad lies, has 1,410 inhabitants per square kilometre; in rural Friesland or Drenthe, near the German border, there are fewer than 200.
Planners have responded by looking at ways of squeezing more people into the densely populated Randstad and other parts of the country where they actually want to live, either by going higher or building on brownfield sites where factories or warehouses once stood. It is a struggle. “The demand for housing is growing more strongly than expected, mainly due to migration,” Hugo de Jonge, the minister in charge, wrote in a briefing paper for MPs in May. The government says at least 900,000 new homes must be built by 2030; the interior ministry has put the current shortage at 437,000. But the amount of new buildings looks set to slow next year.
The reasons are familiar: a lack of land to build on, high interest rates and higher costs. There is another twist: in May 2019 the Council of State, the country’s highest administrative court, ruled that the government’s strategy for reducing excess nitrogen in vulnerable natural areas was too lax and in breach of EU law. Just over 40 per cent of those emissions come from the Netherlands’ large and highly intensive farm sector, which has made the country the second largest exporter of agricultural products by value after America. Its people share their homeland with more than 115 million cows, pigs, sheep, chickens and other farmyard animals, which together emit copious amounts of greenhouse gases.
It was the government’s proposed response — farm closures and a substantial cut in livestock numbers — that provoked a wave of protests in summer last year by its usually peaceful farmers. Seeing their livelihood under threat, they hung Dutch flags upside down on motorway bridges, set fire to hay bales and sprayed manure on the home of the environment minister. Although calm has since returned, the issue has not been resolved.
The migrants are adding to the squeeze: the Ocean Majesty, and the other vessels in use across the Netherlands, are being deployed to cope with the surge in arrivals, accommodating both those who are waiting for asylum requests to be decided and others who have been granted the right to remain in the country but are yet to be given somewhere to live. The idea to use the cruise ship came from an unlikely source: Franz Jr Bergman, 25, and his brother, Luc, 24, whose entrepreneur father is in the travel business and bought a stake in the Dutch and Belgian operations of Thomas Cook after it collapsed in 2019.
When Covid decimated the cruise industry and left some vessels surplus to requirements, the brothers had an idea: why not use them, rather than expensive hotel rooms, to accommodate migrants?
Sitting in the ship’s Bellini Bar, Franz Jr explains how it works: through the family’s company, Bergman Assets, he has chartered the Ocean Majesty from its Greek owners and made it available to the Dutch authorities to house the migrants, who are cared for on board by the Central Agency for the Reception of Asylum Seekers, a government body. The initial 550-day contract began on August 9, when migrants, known as residents, began to come aboard.
At first sight the policy may seem reminiscent of the British government’s faltering attempts to accommodate migrants on the Bibby Stockholm, a barge moored in Portland Port, which got off to a difficult start this summer: many of those the government wanted to send there objected and refused to go, then the discovery of legionella bacteria in the water supply forced the 39 who had taken up residence to be evacuated after just a few days. Last month about 30 returned, in most cases unwillingly, amid protests from Just Stop Oil and other activists.
Franz Jr rejects comparisons between a cruise ship, which passengers until recently paid good money to stay on, and a vessel such as the Bibby Stockholm, which previously provided basic accommodation for oil workers. For a start, he explains, cruise ships are subject to far stricter health and safety rules, which include checking for the potentially deadly legionella bacteria twice a week. “It sounds simple: you just berth the cruise ship here and house people on it, but that’s not how it works,” he says. “There are a hundred small things you have to do every week to keep the ship safe.”
To improve the living experience the residents are put up in outside-facing cabins, with windows offering natural light, while their children are accommodated in inward-looking cabins on the opposite side of the corridor. The ship is moored close to the centre of Velsen-Noord, within easy reach of schools and possible employment. While waiting for their applications to be processed, the asylum seekers — like those on dry land — are free to come and go as they please and spend nights elsewhere if they wish.
Unlike in Britain, they can also work up to 24 weeks a year, although employers can be reluctant to take them on. But there are limits: the decision to drain the swimming pool was not only to prevent children from falling in. With Dutch tax payers picking up the tab, the migrants cannot be perceived to be having too good a time.
The residents on the Ocean Majesty seem happy enough: a 45-year-old woman from Bandar Abbas, in southern Iran, who wants to be known as Saly, is playing the grand piano in the reception area as I arrive. “When we were in our country we had everything,” she says. “We had a house, we had a car, we both worked.” Her engineer husband fell foul of the regime, and so a year ago they fled their homeland with their children, aged 11 and 6, and headed for Europe. Why come to the Netherlands rather than, say, Germany or France? “Someone chose this country for us,” she replies. Someone they paid — a people smuggler? “Yes, they told us it is very good for our children.”
Saly, who trained as a psychologist, and her husband had their first interview with the government’s Immigration and Naturalisation Service several months ago; they are still waiting to hear when they will have their decisive second one. Others aboard the ship also voice frustration at the time it is taking for the authorities to process their asylum applications. Most are keen to leave the Ocean Majesty, move into a home, get a job and join Dutch society.
The various crises, meanwhile, have had far-reaching consequences for the highly volatile world of Dutch politics, boosting support for the BoerBurgerBeweging (BBB) — Farmer-Citizen Movement — a populist party that campaigns for a fairer deal for farmers. Founded in 2019 by Caroline van der Plas, a former journalist with a Dutch father and Irish mother, it went from almost nowhere to win the provincial elections this March with just over 19 per cent, which in turn made it the largest party in the Senate, the upper house of parliament — a real political earthquake. Its support has since fallen back to less than half that, but it is predicted to win the fifth largest number of seats in the Tweede Kamer, the powerful lower house, after this month’s elections — impressive given that 17 parties are currently represented there.
Rutte’s VVD, long the most popular party, meanwhile, is toughening its stance on immigration under its new leader, Dilan Yesilgoz-Zegerius, 46, justice minister in the outgoing coalition. The daughter of a Kurdish father and Turkish mother, she arrived as a refugee aged eight and would seem an unlikely hardliner. But speaking at her party’s conference in September, she said it was not racist to worry whether “the Netherlands will remain the Netherlands” and promised a “fair asylum” policy that distinguished between “real” refugees and economic migrants. She has also not ruled out governing with the far-right Party for Freedom, which is polling around 13 per cent, up from single figures in the summer, making it the fourth largest force.
It is not just asylum seekers who are in the firing line. Pieter Omtzigt, 49, head of the newly created A New Social Contract party, has argued for an annual limit on all forms of immigration. His party, though only set up in August, is topping the polls with 18 per cent, pushing the VVD into second place. Without a change in policy, Omtzigt has warned, the population of the Netherlands will reach 22 million by 2050 or 2060, adding: “Every few years we will have to build a city the size of Utrecht.”
He has criticised the building of “distribution centres” that draw in low-paid migrant workers and urged a removal of special tax breaks that attract well-paid expat executives to the Netherlands, driving up house prices. He has also joined those who oppose the number of English-language courses offered by Dutch universities, on the grounds of the brain drain caused by so many students leaving the country after graduating.
Also critical of official immigration policy is Jan Latten, a former chief demographer at Statistics Netherlands, who is standing for parliament for the centrist 50Plus party, which campaigns for pensioners’ rights. Latten, 71, who was among the pundits on the The Netherlands Is Full documentary, believes his compatriots need to have a sober debate about immigration. In particular he takes issue with the oft-expressed view that an ageing population requires a continuing transfusion of fresh foreign blood.
The problem, Latten argues, is that as the Dutch have become wealthier they have begun to work less — much less: an average of just 33.2 hours a week, the lowest in the EU, according to the latest figures from the statistical agency Eurostat. This means that without the help of migrants the country’s inhabitants are unable to produce the goods and services they want to consume.
“It’s not only a shortage of workers or an ageing population, it’s a question of mentality. It is about the work ethic,” he tells me in a bar at the station in the Hague. “There is a need for more work to be done, but people don’t do it. So we need people from outside.” Government policy, he believes, should be to convince part-timers to work more. The problem is not unique to the Netherlands, but rather a more extreme form of malady afflicting all European countries, including Britain, even though we work an average of 36.4 hours a week.
Such views are controversial and, some say, tinged with racism. Frank Cörvers, a fellow demographer who works at Maastricht University, says it is meaningless to talk about the Netherlands — or indeed any country — being “full”, given that the definition of full changes over time and according to circumstances. “The margins for possible population size in the Netherlands are wide,” he wrote in a recent blog post, “ranging from two million people consuming no fossil fuels and living ecologically in balance with nature to as many as 278 million without agriculture, with only city parks and the population density of the Hague.” The key consideration is about the “rapid changes in population that make citizens sigh and groan, making the country squeak and creak” — in other words, how infrastructure is upgraded to cope with a growing population.
Back on the Ocean Majesty, Franz Jr says his company wants to expand: it is now close to berthing two more ships in the Netherlands, one for a maximum of 900 people and the other for 400. It is also looking to other countries, especially Britain, where Franz Jr has been watching the government’s struggles to come up with an alternative to housing migrants in hotel rooms, which the Home Office admitted was costing £8 million a day in September. “The cost is completely crazy,” Franz Jr says. “Our solution is much cheaper than putting people in hotels. And for families it’s the best solution.” It is also less likely to provoke resistance from local communities, since the ships are self-contained, with all facilities on board.
Later he shows me his correspondence with various British government departments and local authorities. They are interested and want to know more about his proposal but have so far seemed reluctant to commit, perhaps because of the controversy surrounding the Bibby Stockholm. Franz Jr nevertheless remains optimistic and states his company has secured two locations in Britain where a cruise ship could be berthed and is waiting for Home Office approval. “They need my help,” he says.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-s.title: Times Sport Unseen: The timeless power of black and white
https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-s.text:
Marc writes: Bradley and I had been discussing how Gerry Cranham has influenced our photography so we set about both taking images which are away from the action (which we now call ‘Cranham-esque’) and also converting the pictures into black and white to remind ourselves how such photographs are rendered timeless. We also wanted to show that certain colour pictures simply cannot be converted as all impact and drama is lost — this is particularly true of the poignant frames of only using the colour in the poppy on the black and white shirts.
Marc writes: Of course I could not visit Luton Town FC without photographing the permanent fixture of local children playing football on Oak Road. Long before the Premier League match against Liverpool these kids were enjoying a game of keepy-uppy.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF24-70mm lens (set at 24mm) 1/1600th sec f8 ISO 800.
Marc writes: This could be a typical scene outside any football ground and certainly it is a timeless view which could have been taken by Gerry in a bygone age of football. Pints, and pie and chips with not a mobile phone on show — this scene reminds me very much of a Cranham-esque picture.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF24-70mm (set at 25mm) 1/1000th sec f5. ISO 2500.
Marc writes: I think it would be remiss of me not to include this black and white image as two chaps place banners on UKIM Madina Masjid, which is a mosque and a Muslim house of worship on the corner of Oak Road next door to Luton’s home ground Kenilworth Road.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF24-70mm lens (set at 28mm) 1/1000th sec f4.5. ISO 800.
Marc writes: It is my job as a photojournalist to record moments which happen in front of my lens. From the Just Stop Oil protests at Lord’s and Wimbledon this summer to a Palestinian flag being held as the Liverpool team coach arrives on Oak Road, my task is always to capture the sports or news story of the day. This picture has no impact whatsoever if converted to black and white which is why it remains as captured.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF24-70mm wide angle zoom (set at 24mm) 1/640th sec f5.6. ISO 800.
Marc writes: There could not be a more poignant way of converting a simple image into black and white and then keeping the colour of the poppy to emphasise the power of this message.Equipment used: canon R3 using RF70-200mm zoom lens (set at 200mm) 1/1300th sec f2.8. ISO 2000.
Marc writes: This is easily my favourite frame and reminds me so much of how Gerry has influenced sports photography — especially by converting to black and white. Kenilworth Road erupted into a fearsome noise in the 80th minute as Tahith Chong scored the opening goal and celebrated with the fans in the tiny David Preece Stand. There is so much going on in this picture as it is timeless: grandpas in flat caps, kids celebrating with dads and the faces of utter joy.Equipment used: Canon R3 using 400mm lens. 1/1300th sec f2.8. ISO 3200.
Marc writes: Luis Díaz was granted compassionate leave for the previous two games after his father was kidnapped in Colombia but, despite the situation remaining unresolved, he returned for Liverpool off the bench against Luton. And in the fifth minute of second-half stoppage time at Kenilworth Road, he scored to deny Luton their first home win in the Premier League.Equipment used: Canon R3 using 400mm lens. 1/1250th sec f2.8. ISO 3200.
Marc writes: After scoring Díaz unveiled a T-shirt with the message “Libertad para Papa” (freedom for Dad). The National Liberation Army, the Colombian guerilla group responsible for the kidnapping, released a statement last Thursday saying Díaz’s father would be released “as soon as possible”.Equipment used: Canon R3 using 400mm lens. 1/1300th sec f2.8. ISO 3200
Marc writes: This is another frame where the impact is completely lost in black and white. After Liverpool’s equaliser, fireworks were set off above the Oak Road Stand and this colourful explosion of vibrant reds seemed to be perfectly apt.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF70-200mm lens (set at 92mm) 1/1300th sec f2.8. ISO 3200.
Marc writes: Liverpool’s previous visit to Kenilworth Road was an FA Cup match in 2008 which also ended 1-1 and the expressions of these faithful Luton fans show the disappointment of only managing a point on Sunday evening.Equipment used: Canon R3 using RF70-200mm zoom lens (set at 200mm) 1/640th sc f2.8. ISO 2000
Bradley writes: I have loved doing this week’s gallery in black and white. It also takes me back to the days of long hours spent in the darkroom as a boy printing my dad’s pictures. Here, fans walk past a scarf seller who is trading under the bridge that connects the City Football Academy to the Etihad Stadium. It was on the top of the bridge that I photographed Pep Guardiola the day he was unveiled as the Manchester City manager.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3, using 16-35mm zoom lens (set at 22mm) 1/3,200th sec, f4, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: A City fan in front of the Etihad. I like this in black and white but I think it slightly loses the impact of his sky blue suit.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3, using 16-35mm zoom lens (set at 16mm) 1/6,400th sec, f3.5, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: A mural of Guardiola on the gable end of a house on the estate across the road from the Etihad.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3, using 16-35mm zoom lens (set at 22mm) 1/6,400th sec, f3.5, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: Fans enjoy a pre-match meal at the Maine Road chippy opposite the Etihad. I was sad to see the side had been whitewashed because there was once a lovely mural on it. I hope there is another one coming — I think the previous one must have been part of an ad campaign.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3, using 16-35mm zoom lens (set at 28mm) 1/2,500th sec, f4.5, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: A new angle on this season’s Kyle. I have photographed the Manchester City full back Kyle Walker’s pre-match ritual of blowing a water fountain many times but at the weekend it was the first time he turned and blew it face on. I really like this angle and the water dripping from his chin.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3 using 560mm lens (400mm fitted with x1.4 converter) 1/1,600th sec f4, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: Manchester City’s Nathan Aké heads in City’s sixth goal against Bournemouth. This was taken on a remote camera behind the goal. It’s really handy to have a second camera there as the defender was partially blocking him from my position on the edge of the 18-yard box to the right.Equipment used: Canon EOS-1DX Mark ll using 24-70mm zoom lens (set at 24mm) 1/640th sec, f4, ISO 2000
Bradley writes: Hair jealousy again! Manchester United’s young midfielder Hannibal Mejbri in hair-raising action against Newcastle United at Old Trafford. I think this works really well in black and white.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3 using 560mm lens (400mm fitted with x1.4 converter) 1/1,250th sec f4, ISO 4000
Bradley writes: A few unhappy faces in the Stretford End at Old Trafford after Lewis Hall had scored Newcastle’s second goal in their 3-0 win in the EFL Cup.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3 using 560mm lens (400mm fitted with x1.4 converter) 1/1,250th sec f4, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: One of those pictures where I’m not quite sure why I like it — but I do. The Manchester United winger Antony during the game against Newcastle at Old Trafford.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3, using 70-200mm zoom lens (set at 172mm) 1/1,000th sec, f4.5, ISO 2500
Bradley writes: The only bit of colour for me this week is the poppy on the Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott’s shirt.Equipment used: Canon EOS R3 using 560mm lens (400mm fitted with x1.4 converter) 1/1,250th sec f4, ISO 2500
